title: fairsched — Fair Multi-Tenant Scheduling for vLLM: Virtual Token Counter Scheduler Plugin, Work-Based Billing and Go Tenant Gateway

workstreams.title: Virtual Token Counter scheduler plugin inside vLLM 0.31.0
workstreams.summary: Out-of-tree scheduler plugin for vLLM 0.31.0 that implements the Virtual Token Counter (VTC; Sheng et al., OSDI 2024) without modifying vLLM: it subclasses AsyncScheduler, orders admission and each step's token budget by the weighted service each tenant has received, bills only the tokens that actually ran, and never preempts a request on its own. Evaluated on one RTX 4090 serving Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct BF16 (chunked prefill, async scheduling, prefix caching) with synthetic, seeded two-tenant traces, 3 to 6 seeds per arm, against vLLM's FCFS and static priority.
bullets: Built an out-of-tree vLLM 0.31.0 scheduler plugin (subclass of AsyncScheduler loaded with --scheduler-cls; vLLM unmodified) implementing the Virtual Token Counter: per-tenant waiting queues pop the least-served tenant's oldest request, and a tenant that returns after its queue emptied is lifted to the lowest backlogged counter so idle time cannot be banked.

With two backlogged peers on one RTX 4090 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, synthetic seeded traces) where one tenant sends 3× the other's demand, gave the lighter tenant 0.50 of billed service against 0.25 under vLLM's FCFS (5 seeds), and split service 0.67 : 0.33 under 2 : 1 weights (target 0.667).

During a 300-request burst from one tenant, kept the other tenant's median TTFT at 0.39–0.50 s against 28.8–40.5 s under FCFS (5 seeds); static priority with that tenant marked high was faster still (0.23–0.30 s) but has to be told who is interactive and gives one backlogged peer everything (1.00 : 0.00).

Billed the tokens vLLM actually scheduled in each step (prefill at weight 1, decode at 2): prefix-cache hits are never billed, recompute after a KV-pressure preemption is detected from executed positions and billed to a separate system account, and steps of requests aborted mid-flight are reclassified as wasted; CPU tests run the real vLLM 0.31.0 scheduler, KV cache manager and prefix cache with only the model forward replaced.

Dropped an earlier design that preempted for fairness after it livelocked on a deliberately overloaded run with 6,144-token prompts (678 preemptions over 2,036 logged steps, 99.5% of dispatched prefill tokens recomputed); on the long_prompt workload the current design finishes the long requests as fast as FCFS (16.1–16.3 s) with 0 preemptions, and the short tenant's p99 TTFT is 1.9–3.0 s instead of 10.3–12.8 s.

Measured VTC's costs: throughput 0.53% below FCFS on a saturating trace (paired over 6 seeds with the arm order rotated, 95% interval 0.23–0.83%), and the light tenant lost 8–20 requests per burst to KV-pressure preemption against 0–8 under FCFS; an optional kv_share victim order brought that to 0 without lowering its latency, so the default order stayed.

workstreams.title: Go tenant gateway, open-loop load generator and repeated-seed fairness evaluation
workstreams.summary: A Go gateway that maps API keys to tenants and a Go open-arrival load generator drive repeated-seed experiments on one RTX 4090 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct BF16, vLLM 0.31.0, synthetic seeded two-tenant traces) comparing VTC with FCFS (the plugin in passthrough), static priority and a per-tenant gateway concurrency cap swept at 4, 8, 16 and 32. A step-time fit over the per-step log estimates what each tenant's work cost the GPU, and paired seed-for-seed comparisons with rotated arm order measure the plugin's throughput overhead.
bullets: Built a Go gateway that maps API keys to tenants, strips client-supplied fairsched*, vllm_xargs and priority fields, injects a trusted vllm_xargs, always streams, and cancels the upstream request when the client disconnects, so vLLM's abort path runs and the plugin can account the work as wasted.

Swept a per-tenant gateway concurrency cap (4, 8, 16, 32) as the alternative to in-engine fairness on a 300-request noisy-neighbour burst (seeds 1–5, arm order rotated): a cap of 32 gave the interactive tenant a 13–63% lower median TTFT than VTC with nothing preempted, VTC won only that tenant's p99 (0.86–1.43 s against 4.17–6.06 s), and caps of 8 and 4 pushed the burst's finish to 194–206 s and 313–334 s.

Fit each step's wall time to the logged work (prefill tokens, decode steps, causal attention pairs), pairing step k with the interval between the next two log records because async scheduling logs a step while the previous one is still on the GPU: R² 0.997 and a 0.54 ms median error over 29,744 steps, against R² 0.63–0.68 for the other pairings.

Showed with that fit that VTC's prefill/decode weights of 1 and 2 are not this GPU's costs: at the margin a decode token cost 0.97× a prefill token on mixed request shapes (1.49× and 1.71× on two other workloads), so an even billed split gave the prefill-heavy tenant 53–54% of fitted GPU time, and billing decode at the fitted 0.97 overshot to 0.40 : 0.60; the default weight stayed 2.

Measured scheduler overhead two ways: CPU time per schedule() and update_from_output() call in the real vLLM scheduler, where VTC added 172, 311 and 674 µs at 64, 128 and 256 running requests (median of 5 runs, about 0.6% of a 50 ms decode step at 128), and end to end on a saturating trace over 6 seeds with the arm order rotated, where passthrough against no plugin was unresolved (−0.035%, 95% interval −0.10% to +0.03%).

Kept the evaluation's limits explicit: one RTX 4090, one model and 3 to 6 seeds per arm on synthetic traces; the cap was swept only on the noisy-neighbour trace, and on mixed request shapes a cap of 16 stretched the run to 146 s instead of 64.
